cards.example: <input type="number" name="qty" min="1" max="10" required> and <input pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="5 digits"> for a French postal code.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: Inside a <form>, a <button> is type submit by default: it sends the form and the Enter key triggers it. type="button" turns that off for a JavaScript action, type="reset" clears the fields.
cards.example: <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>; a "Show password" button must be <button type="button"> so it does not submit the form by accident.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: Reserved for tabular data (prices, schedules, comparisons), never for layout. <thead> holds the header row of <th> cells (with scope="col" or "row"), <tbody> the <tr> rows of <td> cells, <caption> the title.
cards.example: A pricing grid with 3 plans: <th scope="col">Starter</th>… The screen reader then says "Starter, 9 €" instead of a string of numbers with no context.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: href sets the destination of the <a>. target="_blank" opens a new tab; pair it with rel="noopener" to cut access to window.opener, and with rel="nofollow" or "sponsored" when the link is paid or not endorsed.
cards.example: See the offer: Safari, Firefox and then Chrome (2021) apply noopener by default on target="_blank", but writing it remains the norm.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: <ul> lists unordered items, <ol> a numbered sequence (steps, ranking, start attribute), <dl> term / description pairs with <dt> and <dd>. Each item of a <ul> or <ol> is an <li>.
cards.example: A glossary as <dl><dt>CTR</dt><dd>Click-through rate</dd></dl>; a navigation menu as <ul>; a 5-step tutorial as <ol>.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: Valid on any tag. id is a unique identifier within the page (#section anchor, label target, JS selector); class is a reusable name, shared by several elements, for CSS styling or GTM targeting. An element can carry several classes.
cards.example: <button id="cta-hero" class="btn btn-primary" data-plan="pro">: GTM fires a tag on "Click Classes contains btn-primary" and reads data-plan to enrich the event.

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with this login form?
choices: The password goes into the URL: it needs method="post"
The button lacks type="submit", so nothing gets sent
action must be an absolute URL starting with https://
type="password" does not exist, use type="text" with a pattern
exercises.explain: A <button> inside a <form> is submit by default and action accepts a relative URL. The real issue is GET: the fields travel in the URL, visible in history and logs.

exercises.prompt: Why does clicking the text "Email" not focus the field?
choices: for="email" matches no id: the input has id="mail"
for must point to the name attribute, not the id
A <label> must always wrap its <input>
type="email" cannot be linked to a label
exercises.explain: The for attribute must match the field's id exactly. Wrapping the input is a valid alternative, not a requirement; name is only used when sending the data.

exercises.prompt: Which value passes the browser's native validation?
choices: An empty field
exercises.explain: max="8" is inclusive, so 8 passes. 0 is below min, 12 exceeds max and required rejects an empty field.

exercises.prompt: In which case is a <table> the right choice?
choices: A comparison of the 3 pricing plans with prices and features
Placing an image and a text side by side in the header
A list of 5 steps to follow in order
A glossary of terms and their definitions
exercises.explain: A table is for tabular data. Layout belongs to CSS (flex, grid), steps to an <ol>, a glossary to a <dl>.

exercises.prompt: Two radio buttons that do not share the same name attribute can be checked at the same time.
exercises.explain: The shared name is what forms the exclusive group. With different names, each radio is alone in its group and stays checked.

exercises.prompt: A <table> is the right tool to align the three columns of a landing page.
exercises.explain: A table describes data, not layout: a screen reader would announce meaningless rows and columns. Use CSS grid or flexbox.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for building an accessible contact form in order.
steps: Open <form action="/contact" method="post">
Create each <input> with an id, a name and the right type
Link a <label for="…"> to the id of each field
Add the required, pattern, min / max constraints
Finish with <button type="submit">Send</button>
exercises.explain: A label's for needs an existing id, and constraints go on fields that already have a type. The submit button closes the form.

exercises.title: An accessible, well-tracked newsletter form
exercises.scenario: You are a growth marketer at a cosmetics brand. The newsletter sign-up form in the footer converts at 0.8% and Lighthouse shows 71 for accessibility. You rebuild it with the developer and must track sign-ups in GTM and GA4.

steps.prompt: The current field is <input type="text" placeholder="Your email">. What do you do?
choices: type="email" required, with a visible <label for> linked to the field's id
Keep type="text" and validate the email in JavaScript only
Add aria-label and keep the placeholder, the type barely matters
Put the label in a bigger placeholder, it looks cleaner
steps.feedback: type="email" brings the right mobile keyboard and native validation; the linked label fixes the Lighthouse warning. A placeholder vanishes as you type: it is not a label.

steps.prompt: How do you structure the GDPR consent box and the submit button?
choices: An unchecked required checkbox with its <label>, then a <button type="submit">
A pre-checked box to maximize opt-in, and a <div onclick> to send
An <a href="#"> styled as a button, easier to track in GTM
A <button type="button"> that sends via fetch without going through validation
steps.feedback: Consent must be an active choice (unchecked box). A real <button type="submit"> is keyboard accessible and triggers native validation; its stable id will serve the GTM trigger.

steps.prompt: How do you track sign-ups without relying on the button text?
choices: A "Form Submission" trigger filtered on the <form> id
A "Click Text = Subscribe" trigger, which will also work in French
Count home page views, since the form lives there
Push the typed email to the dataLayer on every keystroke to measure intent
steps.feedback: A trigger based on the form id and a data-* attribute survives text and language changes. Button text varies with translations, and capturing the email on keystroke breaks GDPR.

exercises.explain: An accessible form (right type, linked label, submit button, explicit consent) converts better and tracks cleanly through a stable id and data-* attributes, without ever capturing personal data before submission.

unit.title: HTML: accessibility and media
unit.description: empty alt, WCAG contrast, keyboard, ARIA, lang, srcset, picture, captions, iframes, screen readers

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: A purely decorative image gets alt="" (empty but present) and screen readers skip it. An informative image gets an alt that describes its content or function. Omitting the attribute is a mistake: the screen reader then reads the file name.
cards.example: for a background pattern; for a clickable icon. WebAIM Million 2025: 55% of home pages have images with no alt.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) require at level AA a text/background contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text (24 px, or 19 px bold). Level AAA raises it to 7:1.
cards.example: Gray #767676 on white = 4.54:1, just AA; gray #999999 on white = 2.85:1, fail. Check with WebAIM's Contrast Checker or the Chrome DevTools color picker, which shows the ratio and the AA/AAA thresholds.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: Everything clickable must work with Tab, Enter and Space, in DOM order, with a visible focus. Use real <a> and <button> elements rather than <div onclick>; keep tabindex to 0 (focusable) or -1 (removed from the sequence), never positive values.
cards.example: A menu built with <div onclick> is invisible to the keyboard: replace it with <button> elements. Add a "Skip to content" link as the very first item in <body> to bypass the navigation, and never set outline: none without a replacement focus style.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: ARIA passes names, roles and states to screen readers when native HTML is not enough: aria-label names a button without text, role describes a custom component. First rule of ARIA: prefer the native element; no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.
cards.example: <button aria-label="Close">×</button> gives the button a name. No need to write <button role="button"> or <nav role="navigation">: the role is already implicit. According to the WebAIM Million study, pages using ARIA have on average more detected errors than those without.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: lang on <html> declares the page language: the screen reader picks the right voice and the browser offers translation. A passage in another language gets its own lang. dir="rtl" flips the reading direction for Arabic or Hebrew.
cards.example: <html lang="en"> then <q lang="fr">savoir-faire</q> in the text. Arabic version: <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">. WebAIM 2025: 16% of home pages have no lang attribute at all, so the wrong voice reads the text.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: srcset lists several versions of an image with their width (400w, 800w…) and sizes states the display width; the browser downloads the best fit for the screen and its pixel density. Add loading="lazy" below the fold and a modern format: WebP (about 30% lighter than JPEG) or AVIF (about 50%).
cards.example: : a 400 px wide phone gets the 400w version at 1x density, the 800w on a 2x screen.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: wraps several elements and a fallback . Each offers a format (type="image/avif") or a different crop based on a media query (art direction). The browser takes the first source it can decode; the alt stays on .
cards.example: : AVIF if supported, else WebP, else JPEG. On a 1,600 px photo you often go from 320 KB in JPEG to 90 KB in AVIF.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: <video> and <audio> play native media thanks to the controls attribute. <track kind="captions"> attaches WebVTT captions, required from WCAG level A for any prerecorded video with speech; an <audio> podcast requires a transcript. Avoid autoplay with sound.
cards.example: <video controls preload="metadata" poster="demo.jpg"><source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4"><track kind="captions" src="demo-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default></video>. The .vtt file holds blocks like "00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.000" followed by the text.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: <iframe> embeds a third-party page: a YouTube video, a Google Maps map, a social post. Each embed loads its own scripts, slows the page down and raises GDPR consent questions. Give it a descriptive title, loading="lazy", and prefer a clickable facade.
cards.example: A standard YouTube player loads about 500 KB of JavaScript before any click. With a facade (thumbnail + play button, e.g. lite-youtube-embed) you drop below 20 KB and the iframe only loads on play: <iframe title="Video: pitch the tent in 2 minutes" loading="lazy" src="…">.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: A screen reader (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack) voices the page from the accessibility tree. Lighthouse (built on axe-core) and the axe DevTools extension catch 30 to 50% of issues; the rest needs manual testing with a keyboard and a screen reader.
cards.example: On a Mac, Cmd+F5 starts VoiceOver; walk through the page with Tab and listen to each button. Then run Lighthouse in Chrome: a score of 100 does not rule out an empty alt on a product photo or a checkout that cannot be completed with the keyboard.

exercises.prompt: Which accessibility problem does this code contain?
choices: The first image has no alt attribute at all: the screen reader will read "promo-summer.jpg".
The empty alt on the divider is a mistake; every image must be described.
The logo's alt should start with "Image of".
All three images are correct.
exercises.explain: A missing alt is not an empty alt: without the attribute, the screen reader reads the file name. The decorative divider with alt="" is correct, and "Image of" is redundant because the reader already announces "image".

exercises.prompt: What minimum contrast ratio do the WCAG require at level AA for body text?
exercises.explain: Level AA requires 4.5:1 for body text; 3:1 is only enough for large text (24 px or 19 px bold) and 7:1 is the stricter AAA level.

exercises.prompt: How should this code be improved following the first rule of ARIA?
choices: Replace the <div> with a real <button> and remove the redundant role="button" on the second one.
Add aria-label="Cart" on the <div> to make it accessible.
Set tabindex to 1 so the cart is reached first.
The code is already correct: role and tabindex make the <div> equivalent to a button.
exercises.explain: A native <button> is focusable, activates with Enter and Space and announces its role without ARIA; the <div> with role does not respond to Enter without extra JavaScript. A positive tabindex breaks the logical DOM order.

exercises.prompt: What happens with this code in a browser that supports WebP but not AVIF?
choices: It shows hero.webp; the is the fallback and carries the alt.
It downloads all three files and shows the lightest one.
It shows hero.jpg, because always takes priority over .
It shows nothing, because the first <source> cannot be read.
exercises.explain: The browser goes through the elements in order and picks the first type it can decode; here WebP. Only one image is downloaded, and is used only if no source fits.

exercises.prompt: A video with speech embedded via <video> must offer captions via <track kind="captions"> to meet WCAG level AA.
exercises.explain: WCAG success criterion 1.2.2 (level A, hence included in AA) requires captions for any prerecorded video with audio; <track> with a WebVTT file is the native way to provide them.

exercises.prompt: A Lighthouse Accessibility score of 100 guarantees that a site complies with the WCAG.
exercises.explain: Lighthouse and axe only catch 30 to 50% of issues automatically: they cannot judge whether an alt is relevant, whether a keyboard path is blocked, or whether an aria-label makes sense. Manual testing remains essential.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a quick page accessibility audit in order.
steps: Run Lighthouse or axe DevTools to list the automatic errors (contrast, alt, lang, labels).
Fix first with native HTML: real <button>, <label>, meaningful alt, lang on <html>.
Walk through the whole page with Tab and check that focus is visible and logical.
Add ARIA only where native HTML is not enough (aria-label on an icon, role on a custom component).
Test the key journeys with a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA), then rerun the automated audit.
exercises.explain: The automated tool does the rough pass, native HTML fixes most errors, and the keyboard and screen reader reveal what tools cannot see. ARIA comes last, as a complement, never first.

exercises.title: An online store facing the European Accessibility Act
exercises.scenario: You run the website of an online shoe store (12 employees, 3 M€ in revenue). The European directive 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) has applied to e-commerce since 28 June 2025 and your company is above the micro-enterprise exemption threshold. After a customer complaint, a compliance audit is scheduled in 30 days. Lighthouse gives 61/100 on the product page and axe reports 140 errors there.

steps.prompt: Where do you start?
choices: Run axe on the 5 funnel pages and fix the blocking errors first.
Add role and aria-label on every element of the site to reassure the auditor.
Redesign the whole site from scratch in 30 days.
Publish an accessibility statement without changing the site.
steps.feedback: The purchase funnel is what the auditor will test first. Mass ARIA creates more errors than it fixes, and a statement without fixes has no legal value.

steps.prompt: The 800 product photos have alt="" and the product page weighs 6 MB. What do you do?
choices: Descriptive alts from the product data, and photos as WebP/AVIF via srcset.
Keep alt="": the photos are decorative since the product name is already written.
Copy the file name (IMG_4821.jpg) into the alt attribute so the tool stops flagging an error.
Load all photos inside <iframe> elements to lighten the page.
steps.feedback: A product photo is informative: a blind shopper must know what they are buying. An alt equal to the file name passes the tool but fails the human audit. WebP/AVIF and srcset often halve the page weight.

steps.prompt: The home page embeds an autoplay YouTube video, and the checkout "Pay" button is a light gray <div onclick> on white. What fix?
choices: A real <button> with 4.5:1 contrast or more, and a captioned video without autoplay.
Add aria-label="Pay" on the <div> without changing the tag or the color.
Set tabindex="5" on the <div> so it is reachable by keyboard first.
Remove the video and the button from the HTML to eliminate any risk.
steps.feedback: A pay button that is unreachable by keyboard or unreadable blocks the purchase: it is the most serious failure for an online store. The facade removes about 500 KB of scripts at load time and autoplay is a WCAG criterion in its own right.

exercises.explain: The European Accessibility Act requires e-commerce services to meet WCAG 2.1 AA (standard EN 301 549) since 28 June 2025; only micro-enterprises (fewer than 10 employees and under 2 M€ in revenue) are exempt. Prioritize the purchase funnel, native HTML and product images, then test with the keyboard and a screen reader.

unit.title: Objects, classes and modules
unit.description: Properties, destructuring, spread, classes, this, ES modules, scope, copying, template literals, ?. and ??

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: An object literal is written between braces as key: value pairs. You read a property with dot notation (obj.name) or brackets (obj["name"]), which are required when the key lives in a variable or contains a hyphen.
cards.example: const product = { name: "Headset", price: 89 }; const key = "price"; product[key] returns 89, just like product.price.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Destructuring pulls properties into variables in one line: const { name, price } = product. The spread operator (...) expands an object or array to copy or merge it without mutating the original.
cards.example: const updated = { ...product, price: 79 } creates a new object identical to product but with price set to 79; product keeps 89.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: The most common shape of web data: a list where every item is an object sharing the same keys. It is what JSON APIs return and what you walk through with map, filter, find or reduce.
cards.example: const items = [{ id: 1, price: 20, qty: 2 }, { id: 2, price: 5, qty: 1 }]; items.find(i => i.id === 2).price returns 5.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A class is a blueprint for creating objects with new. The constructor initializes properties, methods are declared without the function keyword, and extends inherits from another class, with super calling the parent.
cards.example: class Product { constructor(name, price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; } } then class Ebook extends Product { }: new Ebook("Guide", 29).price is 29.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: In a regular method, this is the object the method is called on. An arrow function has no this of its own: it keeps the this of the surrounding code, which makes it ideal for callbacks inside a method.
cards.example: In total() { return this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * this.rate, 0); }, the arrow keeps the cart's this. Written as function (sum, i) { return sum + i.price * this.rate; }, this would be undefined inside a class (strict mode): TypeError.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A module is a JavaScript file that exposes items with export and pulls others in with import. Every module has its own scope: nothing leaks into the global object. Browsers load them via script type="module".
cards.example: In cart.js: export class Cart { }. In app.js: import { Cart } from "./cart.js"; A default export is imported without braces: import Cart from "./cart.js".

cards.subject: js
cards.term: const vs let and block scope
cards.definition: let and const create variables limited to the { } block where they are declared. const forbids reassignment, but a const object or array can still be mutated from the inside. Rule: const by default, let when you reassign.
cards.example: const items = []; items.push(1) works (the array changes, not the variable). items = [] throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Numbers and strings are copied by value, but objects and arrays are shared by reference: b = a points to the same object. For a true deep copy, use structuredClone(a), available in every browser and in Node.
cards.example: const a = { tags: ["promo"] }; const b = { ...a }; b.tags.push("new") also changes a.tags (shallow copy). With structuredClone(a), a.tags stays ["promo"].

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A string written between backticks (`) that accepts expressions with ${ } and line breaks. It replaces concatenation with + and makes generating text or HTML far more readable.
cards.example: const line = `${item.qty} x ${item.name} = ${(item.qty * item.price).toFixed(2)} €`; gives "2 x Headset = 178.00 €".

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: obj?.prop returns undefined instead of crashing when obj is null or undefined. a ?? b returns b only if a is null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0, "" and false. Both are supported everywhere since 2020.
cards.example: const qty = cart.items?.[0]?.qty ?? 0; returns 0 when the cart is empty, but keeps a real 0 where cart.items[0].qty || 1 would have replaced it with 1.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: Lea Paris
Lea undefined
A ReferenceError: city is not defined
name city
exercises.explain: Destructuring extracts name from user. city does not exist on the object, so the default value "Paris" is used instead of undefined.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: undefined
A TypeError because a is declared with const
exercises.explain: b = a does not copy the object: both variables point to the same reference, so changing b.qty also changes a.qty. const blocks reassigning a, not mutating its contents.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: none undefined
null undefined
A TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined
none null
exercises.explain: coupon is null, so ?? returns "none". cart.customer does not exist, but optional chaining ?. short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing.

code.src:
const cart = { items: [], coupon: null };
console.log(cart.coupon ?? "none", cart.customer?.email);

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: Guide GEO 29 EUR (PDF)
Guide GEO 29 EUR
undefined (PDF)
An error: Ebook has no constructor
exercises.explain: Ebook inherits Product's constructor through extends, so name and price are initialized. The overridden label() calls the parent version with super.label() and then appends " (PDF)".

exercises.prompt: An arrow function has its own this, just like a regular function.
exercises.explain: False: an arrow function has no this of its own, it reuses the this of the surrounding code. That is exactly why it is handy for callbacks inside a class method.

exercises.prompt: structuredClone(obj) also copies nested objects and arrays, unlike { ...obj } which only copies the first level.
exercises.explain: True: spread produces a shallow copy, nested objects stay shared by reference. structuredClone performs a deep copy and even handles Date, Map and Set, which JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) does not.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps to split a cart into an ES module and use it on a page.
steps: Create the cart.js file and write the Cart class with its constructor and total() method.
Expose the class with export class Cart { } (or export default Cart).
In the HTML, load the entry point with <script type="module" src="app.js">.
In app.js, now loaded as a module, write import { Cart } from "./cart.js"; at the top of the file.
Instantiate the cart with const cart = new Cart(); and call cart.total().
exercises.explain: You first write the module and its export, then declare the script as type module so the browser accepts import, and finally import and instantiate. Without type="module", import throws a SyntaxError.

exercises.title: Modeling an e-commerce cart
exercises.scenario: You are building the cart for an online store with 300 products. It must store added items, compute the total including quantities and simulate a promo code without breaking the displayed cart. You write it in modern JavaScript, with no framework.

steps.prompt: How do you represent the cart contents?
choices: An array of objects: [{ id: 42, name: "Headset", price: 89, qty: 2 }], one per item.
Three parallel arrays ids, prices and qtys that you keep in sync by hand on every add.
A single string "42:89:2;17:5:1" that you split on every calculation.
One global variable per item: item1Price, item1Qty, item2Price, and so on.
steps.feedback: The array of objects is the natural structure: every item is self-contained, you fetch it with find(i => i.id === 42), filter it, map it, and it is exactly the format your JSON API will return.

steps.prompt: You create class Cart with this.items. Which total() method is correct?
choices: total() { return this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0); }
total() { return this.items.map(i => i.price * i.qty); }
total() { return this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0); }
total() { return items.length * price; }
steps.feedback: reduce adds price * qty for every line starting from 0; the arrow function keeps the instance's this. map would return an array, the 3rd version forgets quantities and the 4th ignores this and references variables that do not exist.

steps.prompt: To show a "with promo code" preview without touching the real cart, you need to work on a copy of the items. What do you do?
choices: const preview = structuredClone(this.items); then apply the discount on preview.
const preview = this.items; then apply the discount on preview.
const preview = [...this.items]; then modify preview[0].price directly.
Object.freeze(this.items) before applying the discount on it.
steps.feedback: structuredClone makes a deep copy: the item objects are duplicated and the real cart stays intact. preview = this.items shares the same reference, spread only copies the array (the objects stay shared), and Object.freeze copies nothing: it freezes the array itself but not the objects inside it, so the discount would still modify the real cart.

exercises.explain: A solid cart rests on three building blocks: an array of objects for the data, a class that groups state (this.items) and calculations (reduce with arrow functions), and a deep copy via structuredClone whenever you simulate a change without committing it.

unit.title: Arrays and advanced functions
unit.description: map, reduce, find, sort, chaining, pure functions, closures, Set and Map, debounce

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: map() walks through an array and returns a new array of the same length, where each element is replaced by the result of your callback. The original array is left untouched: it is the go-to method for transforming data.
cards.example: const prices = [10, 20]; const withVat = prices.map(p => p * 1.2); // [12, 24], prices is still [10, 20]

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: reduce() boils an array down to a single value (number, object, string) by calling your callback with an accumulator and the current item. Always pass an initial value (the second argument) to avoid surprises on an empty array.
cards.example: [12, 8, 20].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0) // 40; without the initial 0, [].reduce(...) throws a TypeError

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: find() returns the first element that passes the test (or undefined). some() answers true if at least one element passes, every() only if all of them do. All three stop as soon as the answer is known.
cards.example: const orders = [{ id: 1, paid: false }, { id: 2, paid: true }]; orders.find(o => o.paid) // { id: 2, paid: true }; orders.every(o => o.paid) // false

cards.subject: js
cards.term: sort() and the default sort trap
cards.definition: Without a compare function, sort() converts every item to a string and orders by Unicode: [10, 1, 5] becomes [1, 10, 5]. For numbers, always pass a comparator (a, b) => a - b. Beware, sort() mutates the array in place.
cards.example: [10, 1, 5].sort() // [1, 10, 5]; [10, 1, 5].sort((a, b) => a - b) // [1, 5, 10]; without mutation: arr.toSorted((a, b) => a - b) (ES2023)

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Because filter(), map() and slice() each return a new array, you can chain them with dots to write a readable pipeline: filter, transform, then aggregate. One step per line makes the intent obvious.
cards.example: const revenue = orders.filter(o => o.paid).map(o => o.total).reduce((s, t) => s + t, 0); // revenue of paid orders

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A pure function always returns the same result for the same arguments and changes nothing outside itself (neither its parameters nor a global). To stay pure, copy before you change: [...arr], { ...obj }, toSorted() instead of sort().
cards.example: Impure: const addTax = o => { o.total *= 1.2; return o; }; pure: const addTax = o => ({ ...o, total: o.total * 1.2 });

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A higher-order function takes a function as an argument (the callback) or returns one. forEach() is one: it calls your callback for each item and returns nothing. Prefer for...of when you need break, continue or a sequential await.
cards.example: orders.forEach(o => console.log(o.id)); // cannot break; for (const o of orders) { if (o.total > 500) break; } // OK

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables of the function where it was created, even after that function has returned. It is what makes counters, caches and configured helpers like debounce possible.
cards.example: const makeCounter = () => { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }; const next = makeCounter(); next(); next(); // 2: n survives between calls

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Set stores unique values (duplicates are ignored) with a constant-time has(). Map links keys of any type to values while keeping insertion order. Both expose size, unlike length on arrays.
cards.example: new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]).size // 3; const stock = new Map([["sku-1", 4]]); stock.get("sku-1") // 4

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Debounce waits for a pause (e.g. 300 ms with no keystroke) before running the function: perfect for a search box, a single API call at the end of typing. Throttle runs at most once per interval, ideal for scroll or resize.
cards.example: const debounce = (fn, ms) => { let t; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); }; }; input.addEventListener("input", debounce(search, 300));

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: An error: sort() requires a compare function
exercises.explain: Without a comparator, sort() compares the items as strings: "10" and "25" start with 1 and 2, so they come before "5". Write nums.sort((a, b) => a - b) for a numeric sort.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
exercises.explain: filter() keeps the two paid orders, map() extracts their totals [12, 20], then reduce() adds them starting from 0: 32. The unpaid order of 8 is excluded.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: undefined
exercises.explain: The returned function is a closure: it keeps the count variable alive between calls. Each next() increments it, so the third call returns 3.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: 3 css
5 css
3 js
2 html
exercises.explain: A Set ignores duplicates and keeps insertion order: it holds js, css, html. Spread into an array, it has 3 items and unique[1] is "css".

exercises.prompt: map() modifies the original array by replacing each item with the callback's result.
exercises.explain: False: map() returns a new array and leaves the original untouched. It is sort(), push(), splice() or reverse() that mutate the array in place.

exercises.prompt: A throttle guarantees that a function runs at most once per interval (e.g. every 200 ms), even if the scroll event fires dozens of times per second.
exercises.explain: True: that is exactly what a throttle does. A debounce instead waits for the events to stop before running once, which suits a search box better.

exercises.prompt: Put in order what happens when a search box is protected by a 300 ms debounce.
steps: The user types a letter: the input event fires
The debounce function cancels the previous timer with clearTimeout
It starts a new 300 ms timer with setTimeout
No keystroke for 300 ms: the timer expires
A single fetch call goes to the API with the field's final value
exercises.explain: Every keystroke resets the timer; the network call only leaves after a real pause. On an 8-letter word, that is 1 request instead of 8.

exercises.title: The sales dashboard
exercises.scenario: You are building the dashboard of an online store. The API returns orders, an array of 1,200 orders shaped like { id, customer, total, status } where status is "paid" or "refunded". Product wants three KPIs: collected revenue, the top 3 largest orders and the number of distinct customers. The orders array is reused elsewhere in the app: you must not modify it.

steps.prompt: Decision 1: how do you compute the collected revenue (paid orders only)?
choices: orders.filter(o => o.status === "paid").reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0)
orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total)
orders.filter(o => o.status === "paid").map(o => o.total)
orders.forEach(o => { if (o.status === "paid") return o.total; })
steps.feedback: filter() keeps paid orders, reduce() adds them up with 0 as the initial value. Without the filter, refunds inflate the figure; without an initial value, the first accumulator is an object and the sum turns into a string starting with "[object Object]". map() alone returns an array, and forEach() always returns undefined: the callback's return value is lost.

steps.prompt: Decision 2: how do you get the top 3 largest orders without touching the orders array?
choices: [...orders].sort((a, b) => b.total - a.total).slice(0, 3)
orders.sort().slice(0, 3)
orders.sort((a, b) => a.total - b.total).slice(0, 3)
orders.find(o => o.total > 1000)
steps.feedback: The copy [...orders] (or orders.toSorted(...)) protects the shared array, the comparator b.total - a.total sorts from largest to smallest, slice(0, 3) takes the first three. orders.sort() without a comparator sorts objects converted to "[object Object]" and mutates the array; ascending sort gives the three smallest; find() returns only one item.

steps.prompt: Decision 3: how do you count the number of distinct customers?
choices: new Set(orders.map(o => o.customer)).size
orders.map(o => o.customer).length
new Map(orders).size
orders.every(o => o.customer)
steps.feedback: map() extracts the customer names, Set removes duplicates and size gives the count, all in one line with no mutation. map().length returns 1,200 (one entry per order, duplicates included); new Map(orders) expects [key, value] pairs: with plain objects, key and value are undefined and size returns 1; every() returns a boolean.

exercises.explain: A reliable dashboard rests on three habits: chain filter, map and reduce to aggregate, copy before sorting so you do not break the rest of the app, and use Set to deduplicate in one line.

unit.title: JavaScript: the browser, level 2
unit.description: try / catch, sessionStorage, cookies and HttpOnly, timers, Promise, async / await, advanced fetch, URLSearchParams, custom events, debugger

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: try runs a block; if an error is thrown (throw), catch receives it and the program continues instead of crashing. finally always runs, error or not. throw new Error("message") creates your own error with a readable message.
cards.example: try { data = JSON.parse(text) } catch (e) { console.error(e.message) } finally { spinner.hidden = true }: invalid JSON logs the SyntaxError message to the console instead of crashing, and the spinner disappears in every case.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Two key/value stores, text only, about 5 MB per origin. localStorage survives closing the browser; sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes and is not shared between tabs. Objects go through JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
cards.example: sessionStorage.setItem("cart", JSON.stringify({ items: 3 })); then const cart = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem("cart")). Past 5 MB, setItem throws a QuotaExceededError: catch it with try / catch.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: In JS, document.cookie reads and writes cookies as a single string "a=1; b=2". A cookie set by the server with the HttpOnly flag is invisible to JavaScript: it is the standard protection of session cookies against theft by script (XSS).
cards.example: document.cookie = "consent=1; max-age=31536000; path=/; SameSite=Lax; Secure" sets a one-year cookie; document.cookie.includes("consent=1") reads it back. The HttpOnly PHPSESSID session cookie will never appear in that string.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: setTimeout(fn, ms) runs fn once after a delay; setInterval(fn, ms) repeats it; clearTimeout and clearInterval cancel. requestAnimationFrame(fn) calls fn right before the next paint (usually 60 times per second) and pauses in an inactive tab.
cards.example: const id = setInterval(refreshStats, 30000) then clearInterval(id) when the user leaves the dashboard. To animate a progress bar, requestAnimationFrame(step) is smoother than a 16 ms setInterval.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A Promise represents a future value: then receives the result, catch receives the error, and then calls chain. Promise.all([p1, p2]) waits for all to succeed and rejects as soon as one fails; Promise.allSettled waits for all without ever rejecting.
cards.example: Promise.all([fetch("/api/user"), fetch("/api/orders")]).then(([u, o]) => render(u, o)).catch(showError): both requests run in parallel, so 300 ms instead of 600 ms if they waited for each other.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Inside an async function, await unwraps a promise: if it rejects, the error is thrown like an exception. You catch it with try / catch around the await. Without a catch, a rejected promise shows "Uncaught (in promise)" in the console.
cards.example: async function load() { try { const r = await fetch("/api/leads"); return await r.json(); } catch (e) { toast("Network unavailable"); return []; } }: without the try / catch, a network drop would propagate the error to the caller.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: fetch accepts an options object: method, headers, body, signal. It only rejects on a network error: a 404 or 500 returns a response with ok set to false and a status to check. AbortController cancels a request that takes too long via its signal.
cards.example: const c = new AbortController(); setTimeout(() => c.abort(), 8000); const r = await fetch("/api/leads", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(lead), signal: c.signal }); if (!r.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + r.status);

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: new URL(string) splits an address into origin, pathname, hash and searchParams. URLSearchParams reads and writes query parameters without regex: get, has, set, append, toString. It is the clean way to read a campaign's UTM parameters.
cards.example: const p = new URLSearchParams(location.search); p.get("utm_source") returns "newsletter" for ?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email, and null if the parameter is missing. p.set("page", 2); location.search = p adds ?page=2 while keeping the UTMs.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: new CustomEvent("name", { detail }) creates a business event that dispatchEvent sends and addEventListener listens to like a click. Delegation puts a single listener on a parent and reads event.target: it also covers elements added later.
cards.example: list.addEventListener("click", e => { const btn = e.target.closest("[data-remove]"); if (btn) remove(btn.dataset.remove); }): one listener for 200 rows. Then cart.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:updated", { detail: { count: 3 } })) notifies the header.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: The debugger; statement or a click on a line number in the Sources tab sets a breakpoint: execution pauses and you inspect variables step by step. The Network tab shows every request with its status, headers, payload and response.
cards.example: A form that "does nothing": in Network, filter Fetch/XHR, the POST /api/leads request shows in red with a 422 and the Response tab displays { "error": "invalid email" }. console.table(leads) prints 50 leads as a readable table.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print to the console?
choices: B then C
A then C
B only
A, B then C
exercises.explain: JSON.parse throws before reaching console.log("A"): the catch block prints B, then finally always runs and prints C.

exercises.prompt: In which order does this code print the numbers?
exercises.explain: Synchronous code runs first (1 then 4). Promise callbacks (microtasks) run before timers, even with a 0 ms delay: so 3 before 2.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: newsletter null true
newsletter undefined true
newsletter null 10
An error: utm_campaign does not exist
exercises.explain: get returns the parameter's value, or null when it is missing (never undefined, never an error). has returns a boolean, not the value: true because promo is present.

exercises.prompt: Your script reads document.cookie but the server-set session cookie "sid" is not there, even though the DevTools Application tab shows it. Why?
choices: The HttpOnly flag hides it from JavaScript, which protects it from theft by XSS.
document.cookie only reads cookies created by JavaScript, never server cookies.
The cookie is stored in sessionStorage, not in document.cookie.
You must first call document.cookie.refresh() to sync the list.
exercises.explain: HttpOnly forbids any script access to that cookie: it is intentional. document.cookie reads server cookies as well as JS ones, except those marked HttpOnly, and document.cookie.refresh() does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Promise.all rejects as soon as a single one of the given promises fails, even if the others succeed.
exercises.explain: True: Promise.all is all-or-nothing. To get the outcome of every promise, fulfilled or not, use Promise.allSettled.

exercises.prompt: Like cookies, the content of localStorage is automatically sent to the server with every HTTP request.
exercises.explain: False: localStorage and sessionStorage stay in the browser; the script decides whether to send a value (for example in a fetch body). Only cookies travel automatically with every request to their domain.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps of sending a form as POST JSON with fetch, with proper error handling.
steps: Intercept the submit with event.preventDefault() and disable the send button.
Build the body with JSON.stringify and call fetch as POST with the Content-Type: application/json header inside a try.
Check response.ok and throw an error with the status if the response is 4xx or 5xx.
Read response.json() and show the confirmation to the user.
In catch, show a readable error message; in finally, re-enable the button.
exercises.explain: First prevent the page reload, then send, check the status (fetch does not reject on a 422), read the response, and finally guarantees the button returns to normal even on error.

exercises.title: A demo request form that sends leads to an API
exercises.scenario: You are building the "Request a demo" form of a SaaS site. It sends name, email and company to POST /api/leads, which answers 201 on success, 422 with { "errors": { "email": "invalid" } } when a field is wrong, and 500 when it breaks. Marketing wants the user to always understand what is going on.

steps.prompt: How do you send the data when the user clicks "Send"?
choices: An async submit handler: preventDefault, a POST fetch with a JSON body, try / catch / finally.
A GET fetch with the fields in the query string: simpler and it works everywhere.
Let the HTML form submit normally: the page reloads and the API answers with HTML.
Store the lead in localStorage and send it later with a setInterval every 5 seconds.
steps.feedback: Good call: a JSON POST with the right header is what the API expects, preventDefault avoids the reload, and the disabled button prevents double submissions. A GET would expose the email in logs and history.

steps.prompt: A tester types "paul@": the API answers 422, but your code shows "Thanks, we will call you!". In Network, the request is indeed red. What do you fix?
choices: fetch does not reject on a 422: I check response.ok and show the error under the field.
Nothing: no exception was thrown, so the submission succeeded on the browser side.
I wrap the fetch in a loop that retries 5 times: eventually the 422 will go through.
I reload the page with location.reload() as soon as the response arrives, to start from a clean state.
steps.feedback: Right: a 4xx or 5xx is a valid response for fetch, not a network error. Without if (!response.ok) the code believes it succeeded. Retrying a 422 is pointless, the data is wrong; reloading loses the input.

steps.prompt: On weak 4G, the API sometimes takes more than 30 seconds to answer: the user sees a greyed-out button and nothing else. What do you set up?
choices: An AbortController that aborts after 8 s, a "Request timed out" message and the button re-enabled.
A setInterval that resends the form every 3 seconds until a response arrives.
A console.error in the catch: the problem is visible in DevTools, that is enough to diagnose it.
A requestAnimationFrame that spins the spinner faster so the wait feels shorter.
steps.feedback: Perfect: the AbortController signal actually cancels the request, the user knows what to do and the button comes back thanks to finally. Resending every 3 seconds would create duplicate leads; a console.error does not help the visitor.

exercises.explain: A robust form combines three habits: JSON POST inside try / catch / finally, checking response.ok because fetch does not reject on an HTTP error code, and a cancellation timeout via AbortController with a clear message for the user.

unit.title: Node, npm, TypeScript and React
unit.description: Node.js, npm and package.json, semver, scripts and Vite, TypeScript, React components, hooks, Next.js, ESLint and Prettier, Vitest and Playwright, Vercel deployment and environment variables

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser thanks to Chrome's V8 engine. It runs servers, scripts and every web developer tool: npm, bundlers, tests, the TypeScript compiler.
cards.example: node --version prints v24.x for instance. Even-numbered versions (22, 24, 26) become LTS and are maintained for about 30 months: those are the ones a professional site should target.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: npm installs the packages listed in package.json and stores them in node_modules. Each version follows semver MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: ^ accepts minor updates, ~ only patches, and package-lock.json pins the exact ones.
cards.example: "react": "^19.1.0" accepts 19.4.2 but never 20.0.0. node_modules quickly weighs 300 MB and stays in .gitignore; a colleague runs npm install (or npm ci) to get the same versions.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: The scripts in package.json name the project's commands: npm run dev, npm run build. Vite is the tool behind them: an instant dev server, then a bundler that assembles, minifies and hashes the files for production.
cards.example: npm create vite@latest scaffolds a React project in 10 seconds; npm run build outputs a dist/ folder with index-a1b2c3.js ready for the CDN. Vite 8 relies on Rolldown, a bundler written in Rust.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A layer on top of JavaScript created by Microsoft: you annotate types, the compiler flags errors before execution, then strips the annotations to output plain JS. An interface describes the shape of an object and the editor autocompletes its fields.
cards.example: interface Lead { email: string; score?: number } then lead.emial gets a red underline in the editor instead of being discovered by the customer. Microsoft is rewriting the compiler in Go (TypeScript 7) for builds up to 10 times faster.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Meta's library for building interfaces out of components: functions that receive props (parameters) and return JSX, an HTML-like syntax written inside JS. React redraws only what changes.
cards.example: function Badge({ label }) { return {label} } then : the same component reused 50 times on a product page, with React 19 as the current version.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Hooks are functions that give a component extra abilities. useState stores a value (the state) that, once changed, re-renders the component; useEffect runs an action after rendering: an API call, a timer, a subscription.
cards.example: const [open, setOpen] = useState(false) drives a mobile menu; useEffect(() => { loadPosts() }, []) loads the posts only once, thanks to the empty dependency array.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Framework built on React by Vercel. It adds file-based routing and picks, page by page, between server rendering (SSR on every request) and static generation (SSG at build time), plus Server Components that ship no JS to the browser.
cards.example: app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx becomes the URL /blog/my-post. A blog in SSG is served as pure HTML, hence indexed effortlessly; export const revalidate = 3600 regenerates it at most once an hour (ISR).

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: ESLint analyzes the code and flags bugs and bad practices: unused variable, forgotten promise, misplaced hook. Prettier automatically reformats indentation and quotes. Together they keep the code consistent across a team.
cards.example: npx prettier --write . reformats the whole project; eslint.config.js (flat config, standard since ESLint 9) can forbid console.log in production. Biome, written in Rust, does both in a single tool.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Vitest runs unit tests: one function, one input, one expected result, in a few milliseconds. Playwright drives a real browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) to replay a full journey, such as filling in a form.
cards.example: expect(formatPrice(1999)).toBe('19,99 €') in Vitest; in Playwright, await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click() checks the contact form before every release.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Vercel and Netlify connect to the Git repository: every push builds and publishes the site on a CDN, every pull request gets a preview URL. Secrets (API keys, tokens) live in environment variables, never in the code.
cards.example: A variable prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ is bundled into the JS sent to the browser, so visible to everyone: fine for a GA4 measurement ID, forbidden for a Stripe secret key. The .env file stays in .gitignore.

exercises.prompt: With this dependency, which version can npm install during npm install?
choices: 19.4.2: the ^ accepts minors and patches of the same major
20.0.0: the ^ accepts any newer version
18.3.1: the ^ allows going back to the previous major
Only 19.1.0: the listed version is always exact
exercises.explain: ^19.1.0 means "at least 19.1.0 but below 20.0.0": minor and patch updates get through, a major change (which may break compatibility) is blocked.

exercises.prompt: What happens when the user clicks this button?
choices: setCount updates the state and React re-renders the button with the new value
Nothing: count is declared with const, so it cannot change
The whole page reloads to show the new counter
You then have to update the DOM by hand with document.querySelector
exercises.explain: useState returns the current value and a function to change it; calling setCount triggers a new render of the component, and React updates the DOM by itself, with no reload.

exercises.prompt: This file is TypeScript. What does the compiler do with the last line?
choices: It reports an error before execution: "100" is a string, not a number
It automatically converts "100" to a number and returns 80
It lets it through: types are only checked in the browser
It returns NaN at runtime, without any message
exercises.explain: That is the whole point of TypeScript: the error shows up in the editor and at build time, not on the customer's screen. Once compiled, the output JS has no types left, so nothing is checked in the browser.

exercises.prompt: On a Next.js site deployed on Vercel, which value can safely go into a variable prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_?
choices: The GA4 measurement ID (G-XXXX), already public
The Stripe secret key that authorizes refunds
The password of the production database
The headless CMS write token, used to publish
exercises.explain: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix (VITE_ with Vite) injects the value into the JavaScript sent to the browser: anyone can read it. Only data that is already public belongs there; secrets stay on the server side.

exercises.prompt: A useEffect whose dependency array is empty ([]) runs only once, right after the component's first render.
exercises.explain: The empty array tells React "no dependency to watch": the effect runs after mounting and never again. It is the classic pattern to load data at startup. (In strict development mode, React runs it twice to detect leaks.)

exercises.prompt: For the whole team to have exactly the same dependencies, the node_modules folder must be committed to Git.
exercises.explain: node_modules weighs hundreds of MB and can be regenerated: package-lock.json, which is committed, is what pins the exact versions. Each colleague runs npm install (or npm ci in CI) and gets the same tree.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of creating and shipping a React project with Vite back in order.
steps: npm create vite@latest: the project is generated with its package.json
npm install downloads the dependencies into node_modules
npm run dev starts the local server to develop the components
npm run lint then npx vitest check the code before sharing it
git push: Vercel runs npm run build and publishes the dist/ folder on its CDN
exercises.explain: Create, install, develop, check, then push: the production build is not run by hand but by the platform, on every push, which guarantees a reproducible deployment.

exercises.title: The stack for the new showcase site
exercises.scenario: The marketing team at Norvia, a 40-person consulting firm, is rebuilding its showcase site: 8 corporate pages, a blog with 2 posts a week written in a headless CMS, and a contact form. Goal: 5,000 organic visits a month within 12 months. Two freelance developers are available and the team has to settle the stack.

steps.prompt: Decision 1: which technical foundation for the pages and the blog?
choices: Next.js in TypeScript: pages generated statically (SSG) from the CMS, revalidated with ISR
React + Vite alone, client-rendered: the initial HTML is empty and the posts are fetched after rendering
A hand-made Node server without a framework, every route coded by hand by the freelancers
Copy each post's HTML by hand into the repository, with no CMS and no build
steps.feedback: For an SEO goal, every post must arrive as full HTML: Next.js SSG does it at build time, and ISR picks up new CMS content without redeploying. A client-rendered SPA ships empty HTML and makes indexing harder; a hand-made server costs weeks for nothing.

steps.prompt: Decision 2: how do you guarantee code quality with two freelancers taking turns?
choices: Mandatory TypeScript, ESLint and Prettier, plus Vitest and Playwright tests on every pull request
No tests: it is a showcase site, we will see whether it works after going live
Stay in plain JavaScript to go faster, each freelancer with their own code style
A manual test of the form by the marketing intern every Friday
steps.feedback: The contact form is the only source of leads: an automated Playwright test checks it on every change, before going live. TypeScript and ESLint catch one freelancer's mistakes the other will never review, and Prettier avoids style debates.

steps.prompt: Decision 3: how do you ship the site and handle the CMS token?
choices: Vercel linked to GitHub, preview per pull request, CMS token in a server env variable
A freelancer runs npm run build on their laptop and uploads the folder via FTP
Write the CMS token directly in the code, as NEXT_PUBLIC_, so that everyone has it
Publish from the main branch with no preview, marketing will validate in production
steps.feedback: Vercel (or Netlify) rebuilds on every push and gives marketing a preview URL to validate before merging. The CMS token stays a server-side environment variable: as NEXT_PUBLIC_ or in the code, anyone could read it and reuse it to overwrite your content.

exercises.explain: A showcase-site stack is chosen by the goal: full HTML for SEO (Next.js in SSG + headless CMS), automated guardrails for a rotating team (TypeScript, ESLint, Vitest, Playwright) and continuous deployment that keeps secrets out of the code (Vercel + environment variables).

unit.title: Python for AI
unit.description: numpy, vectors and matrices, loss and gradient, the PyTorch training loop, tokens and transformers, line by line.

unit.title: The AI wrote this for you
unit.description: Twelve AI-generated scripts, each with a flaw. Read, find, fix.

unit.title: CSS: your first rule
unit.description: What CSS does, and how a rule is written: selector, braces, property, colon, value, semicolon

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The basic building block of a stylesheet: a selector, then braces that hold one or more declarations.
cards.example: h1 { color: navy; } turns every main heading navy.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The name of the visual feature you want to change, written before the colon: color, font-size, background-color.
cards.example: In color: red; the part before the colon names what changes, here the text color.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: What the feature is set to, written after the colon and closed by a semicolon: red, 18px, center.
cards.example: In font-size: 18px; the text size becomes 18px.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: One property and its value written as a pair, like color: red; Several of them can sit inside the same braces.
cards.example: p { color: gray; font-size: 16px; } holds two of them.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Targets every HTML element with a given tag name: p styles all paragraphs, h1 all main headings.
cards.example: li { color: green; } colors every list item on the page.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: A file, often called style.css, that holds all the CSS rules of a site, kept apart from the HTML.
cards.example: Change one line in it and every page that loads it updates at once.

exercises.prompt: What is CSS used for?
choices: Styling a page: colors, sizes, spacing, layout
Writing the text and the headings of a page
Making the page react when you click
Storing the data of the site on a server
exercises.explain: HTML holds the content and its structure, CSS gives it its look, JavaScript gives it behavior.
whyWrong: Writing the content is the job of HTML.
Reacting to clicks is the job of JavaScript.
Data lives on the server side, in a database, not in CSS.

exercises.prompt: CSS can turn a heading blue without changing a single word of the HTML.
exercises.explain: CSS only describes how things look. The words stay in the HTML; the colors, sizes and spacing come from the CSS.

exercises.prompt: This rule makes every paragraph red. Which part is the selector?
choices: p
color
red
exercises.explain: The selector comes first and says WHICH elements the rule targets. Here, p means every paragraph of the page.
whyWrong: color is the property: the feature that changes.
red is the value: what the property is set to.
The braces only wrap the declarations of the rule.

exercises.prompt: In this rule, what is color?
choices: The property: what you change
The selector: what you target
The value: what you set it to
A comment for other developers
exercises.explain: Inside the braces, each line reads property: value; The property (color) names the feature, the value (blue) says how it looks.
whyWrong: The selector is h1, written before the opening brace.
The value is blue, written after the colon.
Comments are written between /* and */.

exercises.prompt: Which character separates a property from its value?

Inside the text of each paragraph
In the title of the page
Inside the image files

unit.title: CSS: text and colors

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Fills the box behind the content of an element with a color.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Sets how big the letters are, usually in pixels (px) or in rem.

cards.subject: css

cards.subject: css

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: A note written between /* and */ that the browser skips; it explains the code to humans.

exercises.prompt: Which property changes the color of the TEXT?

background-color
text-color
font-color

text-color does not exist: the browser ignores it.

exercises.prompt: What does this button look like?
choices: White text on a navy background
Navy text on a white background
Navy text, with no background
White text, with no background
exercises.explain: color paints the letters (white), background-color fills the box behind them (navy).
whyWrong: It is the other way round: color is the text, background-color the box.
color: white sets the text; navy is used for the background.
background-color: navy does fill the background.

font-weight: 32px;
text-size: 32px;
size: 32px;

text-size does not exist in CSS.
size is not a property for text.

align: center;
text-align: middle;
center: true;

middle is not a valid value here: write center.

font-style: bold;
text-weight: bold;
font-size: bold;

White
Red
Gray

choices: Nothing: it is a note for humans
It shows it above the heading
It renames the heading
It reports an error

whyWrong: Comments are never shown on the page.
A comment changes nothing on the page.

choices: Green
Red
A mix of red and green
None: the rule breaks

exercises.prompt: Build a rule that centers the text of every h2 heading.

exercises.prompt: Build a rule that gives the body a light gray background (#eeeeee).

unit.title: CSS: classes, ids and links
unit.description: Linking a stylesheet, class and id selectors, inline styles, grouping selectors, which rule wins

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: A dot followed by a name, like .price: it targets every element whose class attribute holds that name.
cards.example: .price { color: green; } styles all the elements with class="price".

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: A hash followed by a name, like #header: it targets the one element whose id attribute matches.
cards.example: #logo { width: 120px; } sizes the single element with id="logo".

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The HTML line, placed in <head>, that loads an external CSS file with rel="stylesheet" and href.
cards.example: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> applies style.css to the page.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: An HTML element, placed in <head>, whose CSS applies to that one page only.
cards.example: Handy for a quick test; a shared .css file is better for a whole site.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: CSS written directly inside an HTML tag with the style attribute; it affects that one element only.
cards.example:
Sale

colors just this paragraph.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Several selectors separated by commas that share the same declarations.
cards.example: h1, h2, h3 { font-family: Georgia; } styles three heading levels at once.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: When two rules with the same selector set the same property, the one written later in the CSS wins.
cards.example: p { color: red; } then p { color: blue; }: paragraphs end up blue.

exercises.prompt: How do you target the elements that have class="price"?
choices: .price
#price
price
class.price
exercises.explain: A dot means class: .price targets every element whose class attribute contains price.
whyWrong: # targets an id, not a class.
Without the dot, the browser looks for a <price> tag, which does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Which selector targets the element with id="menu"?
choices: #menu
.menu
menu
id:menu
exercises.explain: A hash means id: #menu targets the one element with id="menu". An id must be unique on the page.
whyWrong: .menu targets a class, not an id.
menu alone would target a <menu> tag.
id:menu is not valid CSS.

exercises.prompt: The same class can be used on many elements of a page, but an id should be used only once.

exercises.prompt: Which paragraph turns red?
choices: Only "Sale"
Only "New"
Both paragraphs
Neither paragraph
exercises.explain: .promo only targets the elements whose class is promo. The second paragraph has no class, so it keeps the default color.
whyWrong: "New" has no class, so .promo does not touch it.
.promo only targets elements with class="promo".
"Sale" has class="promo", so the rule applies to it.

exercises.prompt: Which line, placed in <head>, loads the file style.css?
choices: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<style src="style.css"></style>
<css file="style.css"></css>
<script src="style.css"></script>
exercises.explain: The <link> tag, with rel="stylesheet" and an href giving the file name, loads an external stylesheet.
whyWrong: The <style> tag holds CSS directly; it has no src attribute.
HTML has no <css> tag.
<script> loads JavaScript, not CSS.

exercises.prompt: How many headings turn navy?
choices: Two: the h1 and the h2

Three: every heading

h3 is not in the list, so it keeps its default color.

Red

Black

p { color: red; } in style.css

This rule targets every paragraph of the page.

unit.title: CSS: boxes and spacing

cards.subject: css

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The space INSIDE a box, between its content and its border; it shows the background color of the box.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The space OUTSIDE a box, between its border and the elements around it; it is always transparent.
cards.example: p { margin-bottom: 16px; } leaves a gap under each paragraph.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The line drawn around a box, between padding and margin. The shorthand gives width, style and color: 2px solid black.
cards.example: .card { border: 1px solid #ddd; } draws a thin light gray frame.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Block elements (div, p, h1) start on a new line and take the full width; inline ones (span, a, strong) sit inside a line of text.
cards.example: Two <span> stay side by side; two <div> stack one under the other.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: margin: 0 auto on a block that has a set width puts equal automatic space on its left and right.

margin
border
spacing

padding
width
outline

Padding

111px

is a block: each paragraph starts on a new line.

text-align: center;
padding: auto;
align: center;

unit.title: JavaScript: first lines

A mistake in the code

undefined

name

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The broad field of making computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing images, deciding.
cards.example: A spam filter, a chess engine and a chat assistant are all AI, built in very different ways.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A way to build AI where the program learns its rules from examples, instead of a human writing every rule by hand.
cards.example: Show a model 10,000 emails marked spam or not spam, and it learns to sort new ones.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Machine learning with neural networks made of many layers; it powers modern image, voice and language AI.
cards.example: Face unlock on a phone relies on a deep neural network.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A deep learning model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next piece of text; chat assistants are built on it.
cards.example: Claude, GPT and Gemini are families of LLMs.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: AI that produces new content (text, images, audio, code) instead of only sorting things or predicting a number.
cards.example: Drafting a product description or a logo sketch from one sentence.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The model is the trained engine; the app is the product around it, with its interface, memory, files and tools.
cards.example: ChatGPT is an app; the GPT models are the engines behind it.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The instructions and data you send to a model; the quality of the answer depends heavily on how clear and complete it is.
cards.example: Summarize this email in 3 bullet points for my manager, in a neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: Which of these terms is the broadest?
choices: Artificial intelligence
Machine learning
Deep learning
Large language model
exercises.explain: They fit inside each other: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains LLMs.
whyWrong: Machine learning is one way to build AI, not all of it.
Deep learning is one family of machine learning methods.
An LLM is one kind of deep learning model, the most specific of the four.

exercises.prompt: Put these terms in order, from the broadest to the most specific.
steps: Artificial intelligence
Machine learning
Deep learning
Large language model
exercises.explain: Each term is a smaller circle inside the previous one: every LLM is deep learning, every deep learning model is machine learning, and all of it is AI.

exercises.prompt: A filter learned to spot spam after seeing 10,000 emails labeled spam or not spam. This is an example of…
choices: Machine learning
Rules written by hand for every email
Generative AI
A search engine
exercises.explain: The rules were not written by a human: the program found them in labeled examples. That is the definition of machine learning.
whyWrong: Nobody wrote the rules here: they were learned from examples.
It sorts emails, it does not create new content.
A search engine finds pages; this filter classifies emails.

exercises.prompt: What does an LLM actually do, one step at a time, when it writes an answer?
choices: It predicts the next token, again and again
It searches Google and copies the best page
It copies a sentence stored in a database
It runs a program written for each question
exercises.explain: An LLM generates text one token (a piece of a word) at a time, each time choosing a likely continuation of everything before it.
whyWrong: A plain LLM does not browse; search is a tool that an app can add.
There is no table of stored answers: the text is generated.
Nobody writes code for each question: the same model handles them all.

exercises.prompt: An LLM looks up the right answer in a database of facts every time you ask a question.
exercises.explain: False: it generates text from patterns stored in its weights. Apps can add lookups (web search, your documents), but the model itself does not query a fact database.

exercises.prompt: What is the relationship between ChatGPT and GPT?
choices: ChatGPT is an app; GPT is the family of models inside it
They are two competing companies
GPT is the app; ChatGPT is the model inside it
They are two names for exactly the same thing
exercises.explain: The app adds the interface, memory, files and tools; the model is the engine. The same split exists for Claude (app) and the Claude models.

exercises.prompt: Which of these tasks is generative AI?
choices: Drafting five headlines for an ad
Sorting incoming emails into spam
Predicting the sales figure for next month
Detecting a face in a photo
exercises.explain: Generative AI creates new content. Sorting, predicting a number and detecting a face are classic machine learning tasks.

exercises.prompt: Asking an assistant the same question twice can give two different answers.
exercises.explain: True: the model samples among likely tokens, so wording and sometimes content change. For stable results, apps lower the temperature and check the output.

exercises.prompt: Which prompt will give the most useful answer?
choices: 3 subject lines under 50 characters for our spring sale, playful
Write something about our product, please
Email ideas for us?
Be very creative and do your best work
exercises.explain: A good prompt says the task, the context, the audience or tone, and the format. The model cannot guess what you did not write.

exercises.prompt: Why can an assistant fail to know about yesterday's news?
choices: Its training data ends at a cutoff date, unless it can search
News is forbidden by law for every AI model
It forgets everything it learned every night
News articles are far too long for it to read
exercises.explain: A model only knows what was in its training data, which ends at a cutoff date. Recent facts must come from a tool, such as web search or your documents.

exercises.prompt: An answer that sounds confident and fluent is very likely to be correct.
exercises.explain: False: fluency and accuracy are separate. Models can state invented facts with total confidence (hallucination), so important facts must be checked.

unit.title: Calling an LLM from code
unit.description: API calls, messages and roles, a stateless API, max_tokens, keys in environment variables, rate limits, SDKs, streaming

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Your program sends an HTTP request with a model name, a list of messages and settings, and receives the generated answer as JSON.
cards.example: A script that sends each new support ticket to a model and stores the suggested reply.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A conversation is sent as a list of messages, each with a role: system (the rules), user (the requests) and assistant (the earlier answers).
cards.example: [{"role": "user", "content": "Translate: good morning"}]

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The model remembers nothing between two calls: your code must resend the useful history every time.
cards.example: A chatbot keeps a list of past messages in memory and sends the whole list on each turn.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The cap on how many tokens the model may generate in its answer; it bounds length and cost, and an answer cut mid-sentence means the cap was reached.
cards.example: max_tokens=300 is enough for a short email, not for a full article.

cards.subject: ia
cards.term: API key in an environment variable
cards.definition: The secret that bills calls to your account is read from the environment (for example a .env file kept out of git), never written in the code.
cards.example: os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] reads the key at run time.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Providers cap requests per minute; an HTTP 429 error means slow down, so code retries after a growing pause (exponential backoff).
cards.example: Wait 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s before giving up.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An official library (Python, TypeScript) that wraps the HTTP API: authentication, retries, streaming and types are handled for you.
cards.example: pip install anthropic, then one call to client.messages.create

exercises.prompt: Where does this script get its API key?
choices: From an environment variable, outside the code
It is written in clear text in the script
The model sends it back in its answer
The user types it in the prompt
exercises.explain: os.environ reads a variable set outside the code (a .env file or the server settings). The code can be shared without leaking the key.

code.src:
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"])
reply = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=300,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "3 blog titles about running"}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)

exercises.prompt: In the same script, what does max_tokens=300 control?
choices: The maximum length of the answer
The maximum size of the prompt
The number of calls allowed per minute
The price paid for each token
exercises.explain: max_tokens caps the generated output. The prompt size is limited by the context window, the number of calls by the rate limit, and the price by the provider.

exercises.prompt: The API remembers your previous call, so the second call only needs to contain the new question.
exercises.explain: False: the API is stateless. To continue a conversation, your code resends the earlier messages, which is also why long chats cost more and more.

exercises.prompt: Your script receives an HTTP 429 error. What does it mean, and what should the code do?
choices: Too many requests: wait, then retry with a growing delay
The key is wrong: create a new account right away
The prompt contains a syntax error to fix
The model is offline for good: switch provider
exercises.explain: 429 is the standard "too many requests" code. Retrying with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s) is the normal answer; the SDKs often do it for you.

exercises.prompt: This file is about to be pushed to a public GitHub repository. Which line is a security problem?
exercises.explain: A key written in the code ends up in the git history and on GitHub, where bots scan for keys within minutes. Read it from os.environ instead, and revoke any key that leaked.

exercises.prompt: Which role holds the permanent rules of your app (scope, tone, what is forbidden)?
choices: system
user
assistant
tool
exercises.explain: The system prompt frames the whole conversation. user carries the requests, assistant the earlier answers, and tool results come back as their own messages.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of one chatbot turn, in code, in order.
steps: Read the new message typed by the user
Append it to the list of past messages
Send the whole list to the API
Display the answer and append it to the list
exercises.explain: Because the API is stateless, your code owns the history: it grows the list, sends it in full, then stores the answer for the next turn.

exercises.prompt: The answer stops in the middle of a sentence, and the response says the model stopped because of max_tokens. What do you do?
choices: Raise max_tokens, or ask for a shorter answer
Raise the temperature
Generate a new API key
Send the same request twice at once
exercises.explain: The model hit the output cap. Either allow more tokens or ask for a format that fits, such as 5 bullet points.

exercises.prompt: You need an SDK to use an LLM: without one, the model cannot be called.
exercises.explain: False: the model is behind a plain HTTP API, reachable with curl or any HTTP library. The SDK only makes it easier (types, retries, streaming).

exercises.prompt: Your app shows a blank screen for 15 seconds, then the whole answer at once. What improves the experience most?
choices: Stream the tokens and display them as they arrive
Raise max_tokens
